articles.title: Southeast Asia’s toxic haze spurs calls for legal action against polluters
articles.summary: ASEAN’s consensus-driven approach and a lack of enforcement mechanisms make legal action difficult, experts say.
articles.body:
Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia – As toxic haze from Indonesia’s worst wildfires in a decade clouded skies across Malaysia and Singapore over the past two months, a growing clamour of voices has demanded legal accountability.

In theory, a patchwork of domestic and international laws makes it possible for Southeast Asian governments to hold polluters responsible for cross-border haze, most of which has been blamed on land clearing by Indonesian palm oil plantation owners.

In practice, sensitivities around national sovereignty, a lack of enforcement mechanisms, and the practical challenges of evidence collection make legal action difficult, if not infeasible.

On paper, Southeast Asian countries are committed to working together to prevent cross-border air pollution under the ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution, signed in 2002.

The legally binding treaty commits the 11 members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to tackle haze, a recurring issue for decades, through “concerted national efforts and intensified regional and international co-operation”.

However, the agreement does not contain provisions for enforcement by a judicial body such as the International Court of Justice, which requires all parties to consent to its jurisdiction, and disagreements over interpretation and application can only be settled through negotiation.

Implementation of the treaty has also moved at a snail’s pace.

The treaty’s coordinating office, located in the Indonesian capital, Jakarta, only opened this April, nearly a quarter-century after it was envisioned.

“For decades, the response to haze has largely focused on diplomatic engagement, emergency firefighting, and measures to protect public health,” Heng Kiah Chun, a regional campaign strategist for Greenpeace Southeast Asia, told Al Jazeera.

“While these efforts are necessary, they have not sufficiently addressed the underlying causes, including forest and peatland destruction, unsustainable land-use practices and inadequate corporate accountability,” Chun said.

Malaysia and Singapore, where haze has propelled major population centres to the top of global tables for poor air quality, have refrained from criticising Indonesia, instead offering assistance to fight the fires, which are estimated to have burned more than 2 million hectares (about 5 million acres) of land in the archipelago.

Jakarta has given mixed signals on accepting outside assistance, with officials vacillating between welcoming the offers and insisting they can handle the fires themselves.

Mohd Hazmi Mohd Rusli, an associate professor and legal expert at Universiti Sains Islam Malaysia, said Southeast Asia’s long-standing emphasis on consensus and noninterference has hampered action.

“Economic interests and diplomatic considerations also play a role,” Rusli told Al Jazeera.

“Malaysia and Singapore have traditionally favoured diplomatic engagement over direct confrontation in managing sensitive bilateral and regional issues, reflecting ASEAN’s broader preference for consultation and consensus.”

Rather than negotiate new legal frameworks, ASEAN should strengthen its existing treaty “through independent monitoring, clearer compliance procedures, greater corporate accountability and stronger domestic enforcement”, Rusli added.

With diplomatic efforts having little impact, attention has increasingly turned to the possibility of countries using domestic laws with extraterritorial reach, an approach pioneered by Singapore.

Under the 2014 Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, Singaporean authorities are empowered to prosecute polluters for activities taking place overseas, with violators liable for fines of 100,000 Singapore dollars ($78,300) a day up to a maximum of 2 million Singapore dollars ($1.56m).

The act also enables the city-state’s National Environment Agency to issue notices directing companies to cease burning on their lands.

The agency has issued such notices to 10 Indonesia-based firms during this year’s wildfire season. But to date, no company has actually been prosecuted under the Singaporean law.

While the legislation allows authorities to identify suspected polluters through meteorological data, satellite imagery, and maps, prosecutors would likely struggle to establish guilt beyond a reasonable doubt in any case without firsthand evidence from Indonesia.

“Such direct evidence can only be obtained if the Indonesian authorities themselves investigate and take action against these very companies and share their evidence with Singapore,” Alan Khee-Jin Tan, an expert in environmental law at the National University of Singapore (NUS) Faculty of Law, told Al Jazeera.

“The most likely ‘defence’ the companies will take is that the fires started outside their concessions and spread into their holdings.”

Malaysia’s government has said it could consider legislation similar to the Singaporean law, but cautioned that implementation would be difficult.

In 2023, the government abandoned proposals for a law against cross-border haze, citing the difficulty of obtaining evidence for prosecution.

Legal action also risks inflaming diplomatic tensions.

In 2016, Singapore and Indonesia became embroiled in a diplomatic dispute after the city-state’s environmental agency attempted to summon the director of an Indonesian company linked to the haze for questioning.

Indonesia’s then environmental minister, Siti Nurbaya Bakar, accused Singapore of not showing “mutual respect”, a suggestion denied by officials in the city-state.

Tensions have flickered during the latest haze season, too.

On Wednesday, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto hit out at countries that “like to insult” his nation over the fires, while pledging to expose foreign companies that he claimed were also responsible for the crisis.

Prabowo said his government took the issue seriously, with authorities arresting individuals found to have started fires, but it would “step up our response”.

The Indonesian leader’s remarks came after a Malaysian politician last week said that Indonesia should be treated as an “outcast” within ASEAN over the haze.

NUS law expert Tan said that while Singaporean authorities could launch a test-case prosecution against Indonesian companies without Jakarta’s assistance, they are unlikely to do so unless Indonesian authorities act first.

“Practically, they are likely to proceed only against those companies which the Indonesian authorities have themselves clearly identified and charged as perpetrators,” he said, adding that a failed prosecution could also expose the legislation as toothless.

“Otherwise, any action that Singapore takes would appear to the Indonesians to be unilateral, and could be politically controversial.”

Eugene Tan Kheng Boon, an associate professor of law at Singapore Management University, said Indonesia’s failure to take stronger action was the ultimate stumbling block to a resolution, but countries could also strengthen their own laws and regulations.

“This could include requiring commodities such as palm oil sold in the region and used in other products to be certified to be sustainably sourced,” Tan told Al Jazeera.

“Customers in the region can also boycott purchasing items from companies that are responsible for the haze,” he said.

“Banks that finance these polluters should also come within the enforcement crosshairs.”

Matthew Baird, director of the Asian Research Institute for Environmental Law, said that stronger political will in the region was needed above all else.

“Governments really have to sit together and work on really good strategic options, like the Chinese government did for air pollution in Beijing, where they were able to reduce air pollution – but it took 30 years and a lot of money,” Baird told Al Jazeera.

“Governments in Southeast Asia have to do it, and they have to get companies to change their behaviour, and that takes time, effort, and probably a lot of litigation,” Baird.

This would involve “holding directors to account, sending directors to jail, holding companies to account, and making sure that they fulfil obligations”, he added.

“Because in every country, it is actually a criminal offence to burn land.”

articles.title: Spotify stock pops on Q3 earnings, driven by premium subscriber growth and AI for personalized experiences
articles.summary: Artificial intelligence helped drive Spotify's third-quarter results
articles.body:
Spotify ( SPOT ) stock rose after reporting Q3 earnings, which showed premium subscribers growing by 9% year-over-year and AI a key part of its strategy moving forward.

The streaming giant posted revenue of nearly €5 billion euros (about $5.6 billion), roughly in line with expectations. Premium subscriptions and ad-supported drove results, up 17% and 10% respectively. Earnings per share came in below expectations at €2.48, less than the €2.80 expected. Gross margin came in at a record 33%, just above the 32.9% Wall Street expected.

"We are very pleased with our performance heading into year-end and view the business as well positioned to deliver improved growth and margins in 2026," the company said in the release.

Shares rose 5% in pre-market trading, a welcomed recovery after falling 6% so far this year.

Monthly active users were up 11% year-over-year to 788 million. For the fourth quarter, it expects to reach 818 million. Revenue is also expected to grow by about 15%.

During the quarter, the company focused on using artificial intelligence to create a more personalized experience, including a taste profile for US Premium users to give insight into their music style. It also launched integration with Meta's Muse.

"By connecting Muse to Spotify, listeners can ask their agent to play music, save songs to their Library, build personalized playlists, find new books, podcasts and more," the release said.

The company also plans to expand audiobooks from 22 markets to 180-plus by the end of the year.

Brooke DiPalma is a reporter for Yahoo Finance. Follow her on X at @ BrookeDiPalma or email her at bdipalma@yahoofinance.com.

articles.title: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq futures tumble as oil climbs, investors weigh Tesla, Meta earnings
articles.summary: Stock futures tumbled as oil prices surged and investors digested the latest earnings from Meta and Tesla.
articles.body:
US stock futures fell on Thursday, led by the Tech ( XLK ) sector, as investors digested earnings from EV maker Tesla ( TSLA ) and social media giant ( META ) while oil prices surged to a five-month high.

Futures for Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^YM=F ) dropped 0.7%, while the S&P 500 ( ^ES=F ) fell 1%. Contracts for the Nasdaq-100 ( NQ=F ) declined 1.7% as semicondcutor stocks fell, reversing gains from Wednesday's session.

Chip stocks fell as the AI trade came under renewed pressure.

Meanwhile, investors weighed Meta's quarterly results , which beat estimates. The company announced a 2-for-1 stock split, giving Class A shareholders one non-voting Class C share.

Tesla shares fell despite an earnings beat , as investors weighed lower 2026 capex against higher spending in 2027 and 2028 on Optimus, Cybercab, and Terafab.

A report that the US and Israel are preparing for renewed attacks on Iran after the US mid-term elections sent Brent crude ( BZ=F ) to $111 per barrel while West Texas Intermediate crude ( CL=F ) climbed above $98. A deadly attack at a Saudi Arabian airport and oil field has put upward pressure on energy prices.

articles.title: Explained: What Double Contributions Convention means for social security benefits of Indians working in UK
articles.summary: Employees movement from one country to another for work usually brings questions around the minimum salary, immigration and taxes.
articles.body: Employees movement from one country to another for work usually brings questions around the minimum salary, immigration and taxes. Such moves can also trigger less obvious social security obligations in both countries, potentially increasing the cost of an international assignment. This was a particular concern for employees moving between India and the UK.Historically, the two countries did not have a bilateral social security agreement as against the other European countries with whom India has a Social Security Agreement (SSA) i.e. Belgium, Germany, France, Switzerland, the Netherlands, Denmark, Finland, Luxembourg, Portugal and Sweden.Therefore, an employee temporarily sent from India to the UK could, subject to conditions, remain outside the UK National Insurance Contributions (UK NICs) for up to 52 weeks as per the UK social security laws. However, once this period ended, UK contributions could become relevant even where contributions continued in India.The position could be even more immediate for employees moving from the UK to India, who could fall within India's social security regime as International Workers (IWs) from the start of their assignment. In practical terms, an international assignment could therefore result in social security contributions becoming payable in both countries.Against this backdrop, social security became an important part of the broader India-UK economic trade discussions. The two governments ultimately concluded a Double Contributions Convention (DCC) to provide a framework for determining social security contribution obligations for eligible employees moving between the two countries. The DCC, which came into force on 15 July 2026, is intended to address the risk of double social security contributions on qualifying international assignments. Here are the key features of this Agreement alongside practical issues which require clarifications.Key features of the AgreementThe basic rule: pay social security in one countryThe agreement is designed so that an employee is generally subject to one country's legislation (UK/India). A qualifying employee may continue under the home country's social-security system where he/she:is an employed person in the home country;works for an employer which normally carries out its activities there;is sent by that employer to the other country to work on its behalf; andis expected to work in the host country for no more than 60 months.Put simply, an employee sent from India to work temporarily in the UK for up to five years can, if the conditions are fulfilled, remain subject to Indian social security instead of paying UK NICs. Conversely, a qualifying employee sent from the UK to India can remain subject to UK social-security legislation and continue paying UK NICs rather than Indian social-security contribution. This is a major practical simplification for international mobile employees and their employers.India-to-UK assignments: Social security position before and after the DCCUK-to-India assignments: Social security position before and after the DCCBefore you leave: existing social security contributions mattersAs per the UK tax and social security authorities (HMRC), to get the benefit of detachment (i.e. relief from double contribution) under the Agreement, the employee must already have been covered by the social security system of his home country before the assignment starts. The employee and employer must have paid, or be treated as having paid, contributions for at least 30 days before the employee leaves the home country, or for the calendar month before the temporary assignment begins.This makes pre-departure planning particularly important. HR and global mobility teams should check the employee's social security status before the assignment starts rather than trying to resolve the position after the employee has already moved.Certificate of coverage: an important piece of paperworkThe Certificate of Coverage (COC) becomes an important document under the new framework. In practical terms, it provides evidence that an employee remains covered by the social security system of the home country while temporarily working in the other country. An employee who remains covered under India's social security system while working in the UK should obtain a COC from the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO). This provides evidence that Indian social security contributions continue to apply and that UK NICs are not due under the DCC. Similarly, an employee remaining within UK social security while working in India, may apply to HMRC for a UK COC using Form CA9107.Employers should therefore make the COC process part of their standard pre-departure checklist, alongside immigration, payroll and tax requirements. The EPFO has also updated its online portal to facilitate COC applications for eligible employees under the India-UK DCC.Five years of social security protection does not mean five years of visa-free workThis distinction deserves emphasis. The DCC determines where social-security contributions are paid. It does not itself confer a right to enter, stay or work in the other country. The UK Government's DCC explainer specifically says that nothing in the arrangement changes the UK's immigration regime or its ability to control its borders.An employee still needs to satisfy the applicable immigration requirements to work in the UK. Therefore, social-security coverage and immigration permission are two separate compliance requirements.An employee could potentially satisfy the DCC conditions for social-security purposes but still needs an appropriate Visa and sponsorship arrangements to perform the proposed work in the host country.What if an assignment is extended An assignment that is extended after it begins does not automatically lose protection under the DCC. For example, if an employee is sent from London to Mumbai for three years and the project is later extended to five and a half years, the employee may remain covered by the UK social security system until the assignment ends or the 60-month limit is reached, whichever is earlier.HMRC illustrates this with a UK employee who’s planned 24-month assignment is extended to 66 months and clarifies that UK legislation continues to apply for the first 60 months, after which Indian social security legislation applies.Waiting period between two consecutive assignmentsThe DCC includes an anti-reset rule to prevent employers or employees from repeatedly starting fresh assignments to extend home-country social security coverage within the overall period of 60 months. Generally, once a detached-worker assignment ends, the employee must wait six months before a new qualifying assignment can begin. If the earlier assignment lasted less than six months, the required waiting period is equal to the length of that assignment.Remote working cases may also includeReflecting the growth of cross-border remote working, the Agreement may also cover employees who temporarily choose to work from the other country for personal reasons, provided their employer agrees and the other prescribed conditions are met. HMRC’s guidance illustrates this with employees who temporarily work overseas to join a partner or to be closer to elderly family members.In such cases, the employee may qualify as a ‘detached worker’ (i.e. eligible for benefit under the Agreement) and remain covered by the social security system of the home country. This flexibility is particularly relevant for multinational employers developing cross-border remote-working policies.Watch out for assignments that started before 15 July 2026Special transitional rules apply to employees who were already on assignment when the DCC came into force on 15 July 2026. HMRC’s guidance clarifies that such employees do not automatically qualify as ‘detached workers’ (i.e. eligible for benefit under the Agreement). For example, an employee of an Indian employer who was working in the UK immediately before that date (15 July 2026) under the existing 52-week period, NIC exemption became subject to UK social security legislation from 15 July 2026, rather than receiving a new 60-month exemption under the DCC. A corresponding principle applies to relevant UK employees who were already working in India. This distinction between assignments already underway and those beginning on or after 15 July 2026 is therefore particularly important for employers’ global mobility and payroll teams.Employees who regularly work in both countriesThe position is more complex for employees who normally divide their work between India and the UK, as the DCC does not provide a special rule for this working pattern. However, HMRC clarifies that in such cases, UK NICs shall be payable on earnings from work performed in the UK and Indian social security contribution being payable on earnings from work performed in India. This differs significantly from a straightforward temporary assignment covered by the 60-month detached-worker rule. As international hybrid-working arrangements become more common, employers will therefore need to review each arrangement carefully rather than assume that the five-year rule removes every cross-border social security obligation.What the DCC does not doThe benefits of the DCC should also be considered alongside its limitations. First, it is fundamentally a contributions coordination agreement, not a comprehensive social security benefits agreement. The UK Government expressly explains that the DCC does not govern access to benefits such as the UK State Pension or change the rules determining access to benefits. Second, this Agreement does not apply to self-employment cases. Third, the Agreement itself does not change immigration rules. Employers should therefore treat social security, personal taxation, payroll, immigration and employment law as independent compliance matters. An exemption under one regime does not automatically settle the others.Areas where further guidance would be helpfulThe DCC and HMRC’s guidance explain the core contribution rules, but additional practical guidance from HMRC, the EPFO and other relevant Indian authorities would help employers apply them consistently. Official FAQs with illustrations would be useful, especially on the following issues.Hybrid and recurring cross-border working - HMRC clearly recognises employer-approved personal-choice remote working to qualify as detached worker. Some practical instances would be particularly useful for employees whose arrangements sit between traditional detachment and regular two-country working. For example, how should an employer analyse an employee who ordinarily works in India but is permitted to work from the UK for several weeks every quarter? How should the position differ where that pattern is agreed in advance for several years?Indian payroll and the contribution base – There is lack of clarity on the “wage” on which Indian social security contributions should be calculated while an Indian employee is detached to the UK. For Indian employees temporarily assigned to the UK, it is provided that employee and employer contributions in India are to be calculated on the total wages, determined under the Indian social security legislation. This raises an important practical question for payroll teams, particularly where contributions before the assignment were based on the statutory wage ceiling (i.e. at INR 25,000 per month) or on employee’s basic salary and not on total wages. A clear guidance on the applicable contribution base that should apply while a COC is in force and whether, on the employee’s return to India, such base may revert to the basis that applied before the UK assignment. Specific examples covering different categories of employees and establishments would help employers apply the provision consistently and plan their costs.Changes in employment during the assignment – What happens when the factual assumptions supporting the original COC change. Common examples include:transfer of employment to another group company;change of employing entity following a corporate restructuring;split or shadow payroll arrangements;a substantial extension in the expected duration of the assignment;transition from temporary assignment to local employment; ormovement from a conventional expatriate arrangement to a recurring hybrid-working pattern.These situations should not automatically be treated as continuing to qualify merely because the original COC covered a period of up to 60 months. In practice, employers may need to reassess whether the conditions supporting the original coverage continue to be satisfied. A clarification from authorities will help accordingly.Ongoing assignments as on 15 July 2026 – The agreement provides that the ongoing assignments as on 15 July 2026 shall not be covered. But that leaves practical questions for employers seeking to reorganise legitimate assignments.For example, can an existing assignment formally end and a genuinely new assignment subsequently begin? If so, what conditions must be satisfied before that new assignment can qualify for benefit under the Agreement? How should short-term assignments (upto 1 year period) that were still within the 52-week domestic-law exemption be handled? These are precisely the situations in which coordinated FAQs and worked examples from HMRC, EPFO and the relevant authorities would give employers much-needed certainty.Welcome step forward, but careful implementation is keyThe DCC is a significant step forward for employee mobility between India and the UK, as it provides a clear framework for determining where social security contributions are payable during a qualifying temporary assignment. Its benefit should not, however, be described as a blanket five-year exemption: eligible detached workers remain covered by one country’s social security system, subject to the conditions of the Agreement, rather than being exempt from contributions altogether.Employers should therefore assess eligibility before departure, obtain and maintain the appropriate COC, and review the position whenever assignment terms or working arrangements change. With sound planning and further administrative guidance, the DCC should reduce double-contribution costs, improve compliance certainty and make cross-border talent deployment between the two countries more efficient.(The author, Ravi Jain is Tax Partner at Vialto. Vikas Kumar, Director, and Pawan Digga, Manager at Vialto, have also contributed to this article. Views are personal. Note: This article is intended as a general explanation of the new arrangements and not as tax, immigration, employment-law or social-security advice for a particular employee or assignment.)You use AI every day.
